body: A dental nurse on weekdays has been teaching this class for nine years, mostly because nobody else volunteered. At twenty past ten on a Sunday there are seven of them on the carpet, one of whom has taken his shoes off for reasons nobody has established, and the laminated picture shows the ark, two giraffes, a rainbow and a great deal of blue. A boy of five who has said nothing all morning asks whether the people who were not on the boat could swim. The other six turn and look at her. She has, by her own estimate afterwards, about two seconds.

What she does with those two seconds is the whole of this subject. She can answer the question she was asked, or she can answer a smaller one that she wishes he had asked instead, and he will know which she has done.

There is a real skill in saying a large thing in small words, and children’s material that does it well is worth a great deal. That is not what this is about. This is about the other move — where the subject itself gets shrunk, so that what is handed over is not a simple account of God but an account of a simple God.

Simple is a folding word. It comes from the Latin for single-fold — one thickness, nothing tucked underneath. A simple account of a large thing is that thing with fewer folds in it, not a different and smaller thing. A coastline drawn in six lines is still the coastline. A coastline drawn with the cliffs left out, because cliffs are frightening, is a picture of somewhere else, and the person who eventually walks the real one will not merely be surprised. They will conclude that whoever drew the map knew about the cliffs and decided they could not be trusted with them.

This dial carries 46 frequencies of 121, and two of the live ones are built for children — one for the very youngest, which is where this article ends, and HM 361.90, Jubilee Kids Party, for the ones just after. They run on the same editorial standard as everything else on the band, which is the point of this article.

Holding that standard is more expensive on a children’s frequency than anywhere else. It means a song that mentions dying stays in the rotation. It means a story that ends badly is allowed to end badly. It means the volunteer on the carpet has to say something true about the people outside the boat, in front of six other five-year-olds, with no notes — and sometimes has to say that she does not know. It is done anyway, because the alternative is a loan taken out against somebody else’s adolescence. Simplifying the words is respect. Simplifying the subject is a debt, and it comes due in the teenage years with interest.

Almost everything made for children now runs the other way. The market for children’s material is not children; it is the adult holding the card at the end of a long day, who wants forty minutes in which nothing has to be explained. Optimise for that customer and you get a vast, warm, competent output in which every story resolves, nobody stays lost, and the rainbow arrives on schedule. It is genuinely well made. It is also, taken as a whole, an account of a world that the child can already see is not the one out of the window.

The oldest teaching material in the faith is not arranged as a curriculum at all. The instructions for Passover assume a household with children in it and build the whole evening around the moment one of them asks what all this means. The question is not an interruption of the liturgy; the liturgy exists in order to provoke it. That design is the opposite of the modern one. It does not prepare an answer and look for an occasion to deliver it. It arranges a strange enough evening that a child will ask, and then it tells them the truth — including the parts about a night when a great many people died.
Children are not being protected from what they have not noticed. They have noticed.

The gentle version deserves a fair hearing, because pacing is a real skill and discretion is not dishonesty. A five-year-old does not need Judges at bedtime. An adult who dumps the whole thing on a child in order to feel rigorous has not been brave, only careless. Knowing what a particular child can carry this year is most of the craft. But there is a difference between not yet and never, and children can feel it. Not yet leaves a door in the wall and a promise that there is more behind it. Never replaces the story with a different one and hopes the substitution is not discovered — and it is, because the text is a click away and always has been.
A child given a God who is mainly nice will meet the actual text at about thirteen and conclude that the adults were managing them.

A boy of thirteen is in bed at half past eleven with his phone, because a friend has sent him a screenshot of a chapter in Judges. He reads it to check it is a fake. It is not a fake. He reads it twice and lies in the dark feeling something he cannot name and would not call doubt. What is actually bothering him is smaller and worse than the chapter. It is that his mother has read this. His youth leader has read this. Everybody who taught him anything has known this was in there since before he was born, and in eight years not one of them mentioned it, and he cannot work out what that was for.

That is the debt being called in. It is not a crisis of faith or an intellectual objection. It is a quiet conclusion about the honesty of the people who taught him, and it is very difficult to reverse, because the evidence for it is true.

The opposite policy has genuine costs and they should be stated. Sunday mornings get harder. Material that leaves the difficult things in is less comfortable and sells less well to parents, some of whom will complain. And an adult who misjudges the weight of a thing can genuinely frighten a child — that is a real harm and not a rhetorical one. Anybody who says otherwise has not sat with a seven-year-old at two in the morning after a story went in deeper than it was meant to.

But the discomfort is not a fault in the standard. It is the standard, working. Children are considerably tougher than the material aimed at them assumes: they already know that people die, that adults are frightened sometimes, and that some things simply do not get fixed. What they lack is not resilience but vocabulary, and a story that pretends otherwise is not protecting them from anything they had not already noticed. It is only leaving them without words for it — which is the one thing the material was supposed to supply.

So the standard on the children’s stations is the same as everywhere else on this band. Small words, ordinary sentences, and nothing left out because it is uncomfortable. Fewer folds, never a smaller subject. A child given the real coastline in six lines can walk it at nineteen and recognise where they are. A child given a nicer coast will one day stand on a cliff edge holding a map that somebody drew for their own convenience.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70. Most of it is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns, rap, ambient and more. 40 are international, hosted in 29 languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. Some are family programming, which here means genuinely safe to leave running in a room with children in it. Safe, in this context, has a particular sense: nothing in it that a parent would have to explain away later.

For the youngest, start at HM 360.30 — God’s Little Lambs. It is Bible songs and instrumentals for the three-to-fives, warm enough that an adult can stand it, with Lamb Songs Morning at eight and Naptime Lambs in the early afternoon. Songs are the form that does the honest version of simplifying. A song has to fit a large thing into small words — that is its entire discipline — and it does it by folding rather than by cutting, which is why the phrases a person still has at forty are almost always ones they were given at four. Three to five is also the exact age at which the shrinking usually begins. Start there and it never starts.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have, and you can add the page to a home screen if you want it nearer. Do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies households are really reaching for — which is how the next station gets built.

So put HM 360.30 on tomorrow while the breakfast things are being done, and then do the harder half yourself. When the question arrives — and it will arrive from the quiet one, in front of everybody, at the least convenient moment — answer the question you were actually asked. In small words. Without removing the cliffs. He will not remember your answer, but he will remember for the rest of his life that you did not make the subject smaller in order to hand it to him.
